subject: physics
title: Progressive waves
key_idea: A progressive wave carries energy from place to place while the medium only oscillates. Its speed is v = fλ, and its frequency is 1 / T. Transverse waves oscillate at right angles to travel; longitudinal waves oscillate along it.

blocks.text: A progressive wave transfers energy from place to place without transferring matter. The particles of the medium, or the fields in an electromagnetic wave, only oscillate about a fixed position.

items: Waves on a rope or spring and ripples on water show wave motion you can watch.
Each point on the wave repeats the motion of the point before it, but a little later.
Energy travels along the wave. The medium does not travel with it.

items.meaning: The distance of a point from its rest position, in a stated direction. It can be positive or negative.
The maximum displacement from the rest position.
The distance between two points at the same stage of the cycle on adjacent oscillations, such as crest to crest.
The time for one complete oscillation of a point.
The number of complete oscillations per second, in hertz (Hz).
The distance the wave pattern travels per second.
How far one point's oscillation is ahead of or behind another's, as an angle or a fraction of a cycle.

items: A progressive wave carries energy, not matter.
Amplitude is a maximum displacement; wavelength is a distance; period is a time.

blocks.text: The wave equation links speed, frequency and wavelength. It follows from the definitions.

items.text: In one period T the wave pattern moves forward exactly one wavelength λ.
Since f = 1 / T, the speed is v = fλ.

blocks.text: For electromagnetic waves in a vacuum the speed is c, so c = fλ.

items: Points a whole number of wavelengths apart oscillate **in phase**: phase difference 0 or 2π rad (360°).
Points half a wavelength apart oscillate in **antiphase**: phase difference π rad (180°).
A separation of one-quarter of a wavelength gives a phase difference of π/2 rad (90°).
Phase difference = 2π × (separation ÷ λ) in radians, or the same fraction of a cycle.

diagram.alt: Change the amplitude, frequency and wavelength of a wave to see its speed and period.

items: v = fλ and f = 1 / T.
In phase means a phase difference of 0 or 2π; antiphase means π.

blocks.text: The two types differ in the direction of the oscillation compared with the direction the energy travels.

rows: At right angles to the direction of energy travel
Parallel to the direction of energy travel
Waves on a string, electromagnetic waves, ripples
Sound, waves along a spring pushed and pulled

items: In a longitudinal wave the medium is squeezed at a compression (high pressure) and spread out at a rarefaction (low pressure).
Particles move to and fro along the direction of travel. The pressure variation moves along with the wave.
In an electromagnetic wave the electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum: c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.
Where the pressure is at its maximum or minimum, the particles are at their rest positions: pressure and displacement are a quarter of a cycle out of phase.
Transverse: oscillation at right angles to travel. Longitudinal: oscillation along travel.
Only transverse waves can be polarised.

blocks.text: There are two graphs of a wave, and they look the same but show different things. Check the x-axis.

items: A displacement–distance graph is a snapshot of the whole wave at one instant. Its x-axis gives the wavelength.
A displacement–time graph follows one point as time passes. Its x-axis gives the period.
For a longitudinal wave, plot the displacement of the particles along the direction of travel. The graph has the same shape.
Zero displacement on a longitudinal wave graph is a particle at its rest position.
A stationary wave graph shows nodes, where the displacement is always zero, and loops that grow and shrink in height.

items.text: Connect the signal source to the oscilloscope and set the time base.
Read the horizontal length of one cycle in divisions.

blocks.label: Intensity
where: A = area it passes through, at right angles to the wave (m²)

items: Energy carried by a wave depends on the square of its amplitude, so intensity ∝ amplitude².
Doubling the amplitude makes the intensity four times greater.
Distance on the x-axis gives wavelength; time gives period.
Intensity = power ÷ area and I ∝ amplitude².

checks.q: A wave has a frequency of 250 Hz and a wavelength of 1.32 m. Calculate its speed.
Two points on a wave are 0.15 m apart and the wavelength is 0.60 m. State the phase difference in radians.
checks.a: 0.15 / 0.60 = ¼ of a cycle, so the phase difference is 2π/4 = π/2 rad (about 1.57 rad).

checks.q: The amplitude of a wave is tripled. State and explain the change in intensity.
checks.a: Intensity is proportional to amplitude², so it increases by a factor of 9.

blocks.text: Polarisation is evidence that light and other electromagnetic waves are transverse. A polariser lets through only oscillations in one plane.

items: Polaroid material is a polarising filter used in sunglasses and cameras.
A transmitting and a receiving aerial must be aligned to give the strongest signal when the signal is plane-polarised.
Malus's law is not needed for this course.
Rope: moving one end up and down sends a wave along it. Each part of the rope moves up and down, not along the rope.
Spring: pushing and pulling one end along the spring sends compressions and rarefactions along it.
Ripple tank: a vibrating dipper makes ripples that spread out across the water. The water moves up and down while the pattern moves outwards.
Use an oscilloscope to find a frequency: set the time base, read the cycle length in divisions, find T, then use f = 1 / T.
Measure several cycles across the screen and divide, to reduce the reading error.
